figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: A-0 in overview. Handheld demonstrations, seen here through their wrist cameras, are the only data we collect. The four parts of the system turn them into actions for robots that mount the same gripper and cameras; the photographs show towel folding on the Franka, the pencil case on TX-G2, colour sorting on OpenArm and the orange pyramid on UR. The chart gives each model’s success rate, averaged over the ten tasks of Section 2.1.
figures.headline: A-0 averages 78% across ten tasks, against 27% for the strongest of four other models, on four robots.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The ten evaluation tasks, each in a frame from an evaluation run of A-0.
figures.headline: The ten evaluation tasks span sorting, folding, assembly and servicing a robot vacuum, each shown in an A-0 run.
citing_sentences: On the ten bimanual tasks of Figure 2, evaluated on a Franka platform at a site where none of the training data was recorded, A-0 averages a success rate of 78%, against 14% to 27% for four other vision-language-action models (Table 1), and it has the highest success rate on every task, from sorting parts and stacking cups to folding a towel and servicing a robot vacuum.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Two minutes of one autonomous run of the robot-vacuum task, with the time on the robot since (a). (a) The gripper takes hold of the first used mop pad, and (b) the second comes off. (c) A new pad is carried from the box and (d) pressed onto its mount; (e) both new pads are on, and (f) the brush is pulled out.
figures.headline: Over two minutes, A-0 replaces both mop pads and pulls out the brush from one instruction.
citing_sentences: Several of the tasks run for minutes: in the two minutes of Figure 3, A-0 takes the two used mop pads off a robot vacuum, attaches two new ones from the box and pulls out the brush, one step after another, from the single instruction it was given at the start.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The bins moved during autonomous colour sorting, with the time on the robot since (a). (a) An arm carries a green part to the green bin; the bins are, from left to right, yellow, green and red. (b) A person pushes the bins to the left, and the red bin is now under the gripper. (c) The arm moves over to the green bin and (d) drops the part into it.
figures.headline: After a person pushes the bins aside, A-0 moves to the correct bin in one continuous motion and drops the part.
citing_sentences: And although nothing in its data shows a robot meeting a disturbance, A-0 acts on what it sees: when a person pushes the bins aside as it brings a part to them, it moves over to the correct bin in one continuous motion (Figure 4).
In Figure 4, a person pushes the row of bins aside as A-0 brings a green part to the green bin, so that the red bin comes to lie under the gripper.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: A-0 on TX-G2, OpenArm and UR, each task in a frame from a run on that robot.
figures.headline: The same weights run tasks on TX-G2, OpenArm and UR, with nothing retrained for any of the robots.
citing_sentences: On TX-G2, A-0 performs four of the tasks of Section 2.1: it stacks three cups and four oranges into pyramids, opens the pencil case and sorts the toy bolts and nuts into boxes by colour (Figure 5, top).

On OpenArm, it performs three: it sorts the toy bolts and nuts by colour, spells YUBI with the letter blocks and opens the pencil case; on the UR arms, it sorts by colour and stacks four oranges into a pyramid (Figure 5, bottom).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: A-0 as one system. Handheld demonstrations pass through data processing into pre-training; post-training adapts the pre-trained model to the tasks it will perform; the inference harness runs it on the robot.
figures.headline: Handheld data passes through processing and pre-training, then post-training, then the inference harness on the robot.
citing_sentences: A-0 is built as one system that spans every layer between the gripper in a person’s hand and the motion of the robot (Figure 6), and each of these difficulties is met at the layer where it arises.
The rest of this report describes how A-0 is built, in four parts designed with one another in view (Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: The A-0 model. Pre-training adds the visual budget gate and subtask prediction to the $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Post-training adds the stage head, whose prediction conditions the action expert as text, and the proprioceptive memory.
figures.headline: A-0 adds the visual budget gate and subtask prediction in pre-training, then a stage head and proprioceptive memory in post-training.
citing_sentences: Pre-training teaches one model the corpus under the objective of See Less, Specify More (S2) [3], which governs what the policy sees and how it is told what to do, with an auxiliary loss on the subtask (Figure 7).
It trains on handheld demonstrations of those tasks and adds two modules, a stage head and a proprioceptive memory (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Where the visual budget gate puts its weight, on 25 subtasks. Each tile shows the left and right wrist views the model receives. The contours trace the smoothed keep probability at three levels, and the view fades where the gate gives it less weight.
figures.headline: Across 25 subtasks, the visual budget gate puts most of its weight on the grippers and the objects they work on.
citing_sentences: Across 25 subtasks (Figure 8) the gate favours the grippers and the objects they are working on, while the table, the background and the rest of the room recede.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Action loss on held-out demonstrations for models pre-trained on a share of the data. Left, during pre-training, with the task instruction as prompt (the subtask instruction gives the same picture): every run has the same model, batch size and schedule, and the 100% run is the pre-training of A-0. Right, during post-training, averaged over 16 task sets: each run starts from its checkpoint at 100,000 pre-training steps, and post-training data and settings are the same for all.
figures.headline: Models pre-trained on more data have lower action loss during pre-training and after post-training on the task sets.
citing_sentences: We pre-train the same model on 50%, 25%, 12.5% and 6.25% of the pre-training data, at the batch size and with the schedule of the full run, and compare their action loss on 3,072 action chunks from held-out recordings (Figure 9, left).
Every 50 updates we measure the action loss on held-out demonstrations of each set, with the subtask instruction as prompt (Figure 9, right).

Averaged over the last 1,000 updates in the right panel of Figure 9, the post-training loss of the five runs follows a power law in the amount of pre-training data $D$, $L=0.063\,D^{-0.035}$ with $D$ in hours ($R^{2}=0.98$; Figure 10): from about 1,000 to 16,000 hours, each doubling of the pre-training data lowers the loss after post-training by about 2.4%.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Post-training action loss on held-out demonstrations against the amount of pre-training data, on logarithmic axes. Each point is the 16-set average in the right panel of Figure 9 over its last 1,000 updates; the dashed line is a least-squares power-law fit ($R^{2}=0.98$).
figures.headline: Post-training action loss falls as a power law in pre-training hours, with a fit of R² 0.98.
citing_sentences: Averaged over the last 1,000 updates in the right panel of Figure 9, the post-training loss of the five runs follows a power law in the amount of pre-training data $D$, $L=0.063\,D^{-0.035}$ with $D$ in hours ($R^{2}=0.98$; Figure 10): from about 1,000 to 16,000 hours, each doubling of the pre-training data lowers the loss after post-training by about 2.4%.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Streaming decoding with two slots. Left: the buffer before and after one query. Right: the noise level of one chunk on its way through the buffer, with a uniform schedule and with the non-uniform schedule used in A-0.
figures.headline: With two slots, the non-uniform schedule makes the final update a small correction from 0.1 to 0.
citing_sentences: At each query the action expert denoises the whole buffer on the newest observation: the chunk in slot $k$ moves from $\ell_{k}$ to $\ell_{k-1}$, the first comes out clean and is executed, and fresh noise enters at the back (Figure 11, left).
We propose non-uniform streaming decoding, which makes the size of an update depend on how far the chunk is from execution (Figure 11, right).

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: The loss in the right panel of Figure 9 for each of the 16 task sets.
figures.headline: Post-training loss for each of the 16 task sets, with the smallest pre-training share highest on all 16.
citing_sentences: Set by set (Figure 12 in the appendix), the smallest share has the highest loss on all 16.
Figure 12 gives the post-training loss in the right panel of Figure 9 for each of the 16 task sets (Section 4.6).

abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

sections.body: The introduction states the problem: handheld grippers let data grow with the number of people recording it, but the policy sees only through wrist cameras and must work at sites absent from its data. A-0 uses handheld demonstrations for pre-training and post-training, with no teleoperation, reinforcement learning, on-robot corrections or simulation. On ten evaluation tasks it averages 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other models post-trained on the same demonstrations. The section lists four contributions: the system, the open release of the dataset, weights and recipe, long tasks run from one instruction through two wrist cameras, and operation on several robots that take the same gripper.
sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.headline: A-0 learns bimanual manipulation from 16,151 hours of handheld gripper demonstrations, with no robot data at any stage.

sections.body: The results cover ten bimanual tasks evaluated on a Franka platform at a site where none of the training data was recorded. Each task gets one instruction and is scored over 15 trials with partial credit. A-0 uses one recipe for all tasks, while each of the four other models uses its best setting per task, across several action horizons, action frequencies and update counts. Table 1 shows A-0 with the highest success rate on every task, averaging 78% against 14% to 27% for the others. Earbuds is the lowest A-0 result at 30%. The section also reports that when a person moves the bins, A-0 reaches the correct bin in one continuous motion, and that the same weights run on TX-G2, OpenArm and UR.
sections.heading: 2. Results
sections.headline: On ten tasks at an unseen site, A-0 averages 78% success and tops every task against four other models.

sections.body: Data comes from the YUBI handheld gripper, which has a wrist camera, finger-driven jaws and six-degree-of-freedom tracking, and mounts on a robot arm as its end effector. The corpus holds 16,151 hours of bimanual demonstrations covering well over a hundred tasks, with 1.74 billion time steps at 30 Hz. Each demonstration is split into subtasks averaging 5.5 seconds, and each segment carries a task instruction and a subtask instruction. Before training, demonstrations pass through filtering, outlier detection and retiming. Table 2 lists the contents: two wrist cameras, and the pose and opening of each gripper as proprioception.
sections.heading: 3. Data
sections.headline: The corpus holds 16,151 hours of bimanual YUBI demonstrations split into 10.65 million subtask segments.

sections.body: Pre-training uses the See Less, Specify More objective with an auxiliary subtask loss, on a backbone initialised from the public pi0.5 base checkpoint. It is trained for 300,000 steps at batch size 2,048. Two 224×224 wrist images, an instruction and a state go in, and a chunk of 32 anchored actions on a 20 Hz grid comes out. A visual budget gate scores each image token against the instruction and holds the mean keep probability to a target. Across 25 subtasks the gate favours the grippers and the objects they work on. Runs on 50%, 25%, 12.5% and 6.25% of the data show that more data gives lower action loss, and a power-law fit from about 1,000 to 16,000 hours has R² of 0.98.
sections.heading: 4. Pre-training
sections.headline: Pre-training on more handheld data lowers post-training loss, each doubling cutting it by about 2.4%.

sections.body: Post-training adapts the pre-trained model to long tasks with one recipe for every task. A stage head predicts the current stage from the backbone representation, and the predicted stage is passed to the action expert as language. A proprioceptive memory holds the last ten states with their elapsed times, which four learned queries compress into four tokens. Training samples the history at 5 to 15 Hz and withholds it a quarter of the time, so the policy can act without it. The gate keeps a budget of 0.9 and also acts on attention. The objective adds stage and subtask terms with weights 0.1 and 0.01. Table 4 gives the full recipe, including 20,000 updates at batch size 64.
sections.heading: 5. Post-training
sections.headline: Post-training adds a stage head and a memory of the last ten states, and takes under four hours on eight H200 GPUs.

sections.body: The inference harness turns predictions into continuous motion with two components. Stage smoothing conditions the action expert on the most probable stage under a moving average of the predicted probabilities, so one wrong prediction barely moves it. Non-uniform streaming decoding holds a buffer of chunks at staggered noise levels. A-0 uses two slots with levels 0.1 and 1, so a chunk takes a large step into the buffer and only a small correction just before it runs. In steady state the action expert is evaluated twice, against ten times for standard decoding, and a query takes about 60 ms on an H200 GPU. With evenly spaced levels, few slots leave seams between chunks and many slots slow the response to scene changes.
sections.heading: 6. Inference Harness
sections.headline: The harness smooths the predicted stage and decodes actions as a continuous stream with a non-uniform noise schedule.

sections.body: Related work covers handheld data collection, vision-language-action models trained on robot data, language for long tasks, selective perception and real-time action generation. The section places A-0 against each of these. It builds on the UMI relative-trajectory representation and on FlashVLA streaming, starts from the pi0.5 architecture and its public weights, and follows S2 in pre-training. It states that A-0 collects no robot demonstrations and no on-robot experience. The non-uniform schedule and its adaptation to anchored actions and stage-conditioned policies are presented as the additions of this work.
sections.heading: 7. Related Work
sections.headline: A-0 builds on prior handheld collection and FlashVLA streaming, and adds no robot demonstrations.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the system as one pipeline, from data processing through pre-training and post-training to the inference harness on the robot. It states that A-0 carries out long, precise tasks from a single instruction through two wrist cameras, at a site outside its data, with no robot data collected. It also states that A-0 runs on robots that carry the same grippers. The corpus is described as still growing, and A-0 as the first system built on it. The section reports no new results and restates no limits beyond those given earlier.
sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.headline: A-0 is the first system built on a corpus that is still growing, and it runs on robots carrying YUBI.

sections.body: The appendix contains one figure, Figure 12, which gives the post-training loss from the right panel of Figure 9 for each of the 16 task sets. It is referred to from Section 4.6. Set by set, the smallest pre-training share has the highest loss on all 16 sets. The appendix adds no method, data or results beyond these set-by-set curves.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives the post-training loss for each of the 16 task sets.
